whatItIs.text: A rhizome of the ginger family, boiled, dried, and ground into the deep yellow powder that colours curries — and, as curcumin, an approved food colouring worldwide.

historyNote.text: Turmeric was first used as a dye and spread with Hinduism and Buddhism — it colours monks' and priests' robes; Austronesian peoples carried it from Taiwan's dispersal (from about 3000 BC) into Southeast Asia and Oceania, using it for food, medicine, textiles, and body paint.

howToChoose.text: Choose brightly coloured powder with an earthy, mustard-like aroma — faded colour means faded flavour; fresh turmeric root (like a slim ginger hand) is worth grating when you find it.

storage.text: Keep sealed, dark, and dry; it stains everything, including containers. The rulebook has the details.

foodSafetyRef.note: spice storage guidance lives in the food-safety rulebook

useItUp.text: Bloom turmeric in fat or toast it into rice and lentils for colour and depth; a whisk of it into eggs or mustard makes everything look golden.
